prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: I opened with magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, but having read the colleagues' arguments I now put topological insulators first. The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators define a state of matter by topology rather than symmetry breaking. The chain from theory to experiment is traceable: Kane and Mele proposed the Z2 classification and the graphene quantum spin Hall idea, and Molenkamp's HgTe quantum wells gave the decisive transport measurement of protected edge channels, with conductance quantised as predicted. Later ARPES on Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 and first-principles band-structure calculations agree on the surface states, which is the kind of independent, quantitative theory-experiment agreement I value. Fifteen years of confirmation by many groups give a stable interpretation, and the concept has spread to photonics, cold atoms and phononics. Two members ranked it first, and the opening statements call recognition overdue rather than premature, which is the opposite of my concern about twisted bilayer graphene.
statement.case_against: The credit is the hard part. A three-name cap leaves out Hasan, whose group made the first 3D topological insulator spectroscopy, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that guided the HgTe experiment is outside the supplied names, with S.-C. Zhang deceased. Whichever trio is chosen is open to dispute, and the 2D versus 3D history may argue for a different split. The 2016 prize already honoured topological phases (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz), so the committee must be convinced that this is a distinct and fresh discovery, not a continuation. Twisted bilayer graphene, by comparison, is the more novel platform, but its superconducting pairing is unsettled and it is only about eight years old.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B040 first as a clean, general mechanism in which a topological invariant protects edge or surface states, with overdue recognition, and proposes Kane, Mele and Molenkamp while noting that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang priority and the 2D/3D split are unresolved.
responses.response: I agree on the maturity and on the trio. Your point about overdue recognition made me weigh B040 above B038, which you ranked third on timing grounds as well. I would qualify one thing: the HgTe result needs the BHZ proposal, so the citation should speak of the experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect, not of a single decisive theory paper, and the committee should record explicitly why BHZ is not credited.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B040 first but proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, because the 3D surface-state spectroscopy is a decisive measurement. She calls Mele's omission hard to justify.
responses.response: I take the Hasan argument seriously, since ARPES is exactly the kind of spectroscopic link between experiment and calculation that persuades me. But dropping Mele is hard to defend: Kane and Mele wrote the 2005 Z2 papers together, and the 3D classification builds on that. If we keep three seats, I would keep the theory pair plus Molenkamp, who gave the first decisive realisation. If the committee thinks the 3D discovery is essential, then I would consider asking whether Hasan can replace Molenkamp, though I think that weakens the clear quantum spin Hall narrative.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a measurement breakthrough with many independent labs at the 1e-18 level and a clean two-person credit, and he is cautious about the overlap with the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I accept that B045 is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and thoroughly confirmed, and I keep it as an alternative. My reservation is that its discovery content is a precision-measurement tool rather than a new state of matter, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. I would be comfortable if the committee preferred it, but I do not think it should outrank a condensed-matter discovery of this breadth.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, a clean strong-coupling demonstration reproduced across many laboratories, but he flags his own close ties to that community and the delicate timing after the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I respect the scientific case and your candid conflict flag. I defer to you on the physics of cQED, but I share your timing concern: a second superconducting-circuit prize one year after the first is hard to justify when other mature fields wait. I would prefer to see B026 considered after a longer gap.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as a new observational window, with confirmation across channels and a clean two-person credit, though he notes the allocation question around the large collaboration.
responses.response: This is outside my expertise, so I defer to you and Pearce on the detector side. I note the cleaner two-name credit and the strong maturity argument. I would want to hear whether Halzen and Karle capture the decisive contributions before I could support it over B040.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can justify a trio that omits Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and whether a two-part 2D/3D split would be fairer.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize makes B040 look like a continuation rather than a new discovery.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene will look more mature by the time of a final ballot, given the unresolved pairing mechanism.
Priority claims of earlier moire theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) bear on B038 and I cannot verify them from the supplied text.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I work on electronic-structure theory and magnetism at Uppsala, and have no stated link to the credited people of any shortlisted candidate. I chaired the 2025 committee, which is not a conflict.
